Content:
Why do we study derivatives? It turns out that we can use derivatives to understand many practical situations, like the motion of a particle.

Content:
Suppose we're given the position [MATH: x] of a particle as a function of time, so [MATH: x = x(t).] The velocity [MATH: v(t)] of the particle is the rate of change of its position with respect to time.

Content:
So, we can compute the velocity by taking the derivative of [MATH: x(t)] with respect to time:
[MATH: v(t) = \frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}]

Content:
The velocity of a particle represents how fast the particle is going at any moment in time, and the direction in which it is traveling (positive or negative).

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's build some more intuition for why velocity is defined as the derivative of position.

Content:
If a car is moving at a constant velocity, and it travels a distance of [MATH: \Delta x=100\,\textrm{m}] in a time interval [MATH: \Delta t=10\,\textrm{s},] then we know that its velocity is given by

Content:
[MATH: v|= (Δx)/(Δt); = (100)/(10); = 10m/s.]

Content:
But what if the velocity itself changes with time? Perhaps the car accelerates for a couple of seconds in the beginning, thereby increasing its velocity. In that case, the formula above only gives us the average velocity.

Content:
However, if we take a smaller time interval, we can get more precise information about the velocity at a given time [MATH: t.] To get the instantaneous velocity of the car, we need to take the limit as [MATH: \Delta t\to 0.] When we do this, we get the derivative:

Content:
[MATH: v(t)|= lim_(Δt → 0)(Δx)/(Δt); = (dx)/(dt)]

Content:
The instantaneous velocity is the number that you read on the speedometer of cars.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function: [MATH: v(t)|= (dx)/(dt); = (d)/(dt)(6t^{4} − 3t^{2} + t); = 24t^{3} − 6t + 1] To calculate the velocity at [MATH: t=1,] we substitute [MATH: t=1] into the velocity function above: [MATH: v(1)|= 24(1)^{3} − 6(1) + 1; = 24 − 6 + 1; = 19]

Therefore, the velocity of the particle is [MATH: 19\,\textrm{m/s}.]

items.title: Speed vs Velocity

sections.normalized_html: Speed, however, is a scalar quantity with no direction. It is the magnitude of the velocity, given by [MATH: |v|]. The speed is always positive or zero, and is never negative.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Why do we study derivatives? It turns out that we can use derivatives to understand many practical situations, like the motion of a particle.

Content:
Suppose we're given the position [MATH: x] of a particle as a function of time, so [MATH: x = x(t).] The velocity [MATH: v(t)] of the particle is the rate of change of its position with respect to time.

Content:
So, we can compute the velocity by taking the derivative of [MATH: x(t)] with respect to time:
[MATH: v(t) = \frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}]

Content:
The velocity of a particle represents how fast the particle is going at any moment in time, and the direction in which it is traveling (positive or negative).

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/41c191f9cf62f9a6230b07b59873510b]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle

Example Prompt:
The position [MATH: x] of a particle at time [MATH: t] is given by [MATH: x(t) = 3t^2 +3t +1.] Calculate the velocity at time [MATH: t.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function [MATH: x(t)] with respect to time:
[MATH: v(t)|= (dx)/(dt); = (d)/(dt)(3t^{2} + 3t + 1); = 6t + 3]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Intuition Behind the Definition

Content:
Let's build some more intuition for why velocity is defined as the derivative of position.

Content:
If a car is moving at a constant velocity, and it travels a distance of [MATH: \Delta x=100\,\textrm{m}] in a time interval [MATH: \Delta t=10\,\textrm{s},] then we know that its velocity is given by

Content:
[MATH: v|= (Δx)/(Δt); = (100)/(10); = 10m/s.]

Content:
But what if the velocity itself changes with time? Perhaps the car accelerates for a couple of seconds in the beginning, thereby increasing its velocity. In that case, the formula above only gives us the average velocity.

Content:
However, if we take a smaller time interval, we can get more precise information about the velocity at a given time [MATH: t.] To get the instantaneous velocity of the car, we need to take the limit as [MATH: \Delta t\to 0.] When we do this, we get the derivative:

Content:
[MATH: v(t)|= lim_(Δt → 0)(Δx)/(Δt); = (dx)/(dt)]

Content:
The instantaneous velocity is the number that you read on the speedometer of cars.

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at a Particular Moment

Example Prompt:
The position [MATH: x,] measured in meters, of a particle at time [MATH: t] is given by [MATH: x(t) = 6t^4 -3t^2 +t,] where [MATH: t] is the time in seconds. Calculate the velocity at time [MATH: t=1].

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:
[MATH: v(t)|= (dx)/(dt); = (d)/(dt)(6t^{4} − 3t^{2} + t); = 24t^{3} − 6t + 1]
To calculate the velocity at [MATH: t=1,] we substitute [MATH: t=1] into the velocity function above:
[MATH: v(1)|= 24(1)^{3} − 6(1) + 1; = 24 − 6 + 1; = 19]

Therefore, the velocity of the particle is [MATH: 19\,\textrm{m/s}.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Speed vs Velocity

Content:
Velocity is a vector. It has both magnitude and direction, and can be negative. For motion along a straight line (i.e. along the [MATH: x]-axis), negative velocity means that it's moving to the left, in the negative direction.

Content:
Speed, however, is a scalar quantity with no direction. It is the magnitude of the velocity, given by [MATH: |v|]. The speed is always positive or zero, and is never negative.

Content:
For example, if a particle moving along the [MATH: x]-axis has a velocity of [MATH: -2 \, \textrm{m/s},] then it is moving left (in the negative direction) with a speed of [MATH: |{-2}|=2 \, \textrm{m/s}.]

Content:
The reason why we take the absolute value when computing speed is that speed is directionless (unlike velocity, which can be positive or negative depending on the direction of motion).

Item 10 — Example: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Particular Moment

Example Prompt:
The position [MATH: s(t)] of a particle (in meters) at time [MATH: t] seconds is given by
[MATH: s(t) = t^2 - 36t,\quad t\geq 0.]
Calculate the speed of the particle when [MATH: t=1\,\textrm{s}].

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:
[MATH: v(t)|= (ds)/(dt); = (d)/(dt)(t^{2} − 36t); = 2t − 36]
When [MATH: t=1,] the velocity is
[MATH: v(1) = 2(1) - 36 = -34.]
Therefore, the speed is [MATH: |{-34}| = 34\, \textrm{m/s}.]
